new_candidates.body:
## Environment
* OS Version: Ubuntu 24.04
* Source or binary build? Source. `gz-sim8` (8.15.0 plus later commits) and `main` (3c9c865c). The code is the same in both.

## Description
* Expected behavior: A model that starts at rest publishes a twist of zero from the first odometry message on, wherever it is placed.
* Actual behavior: The first messages carry a large twist when the model does not start at the origin. The error is the distance to the origin divided by the time step.

In a test world with a model at rest at `3 -2 1` with a yaw of 0.7 rad, a 1 ms step and `<odom_publish_frequency>1000</odom_publish_frequency>`, the first messages have:

```
message  linear x   linear y   angular z
0        1006.1    -3462.3     700.0
1         503.0    -1731.2     350.0
2         335.4    -1154.1     233.3
3         251.5     -865.6     175.0
```

The values are the first sample divided by 1, 2, 3, 4, because the rolling mean has only the samples it has seen so far. On a legged robot model that starts away from the origin we saw a first linear velocity of `(1600, -2080, 640)` m/s.

## Cause
`OdometryPublisherPrivate::UpdateOdometry` runs a first call that only sets `lastUpdateTime` and returns. `lastUpdatePose` keeps its default value (identity at the origin). The next call computes the displacement as `pose - lastUpdatePose`, which is the whole pose of the model, and divides it by one time step. A yaw other than zero gives the same error in the angular velocity.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Load a world with a model at a pose away from the origin, for example `<pose>3 -2 1 0 0 0.7</pose>`, that nothing moves, and an `OdometryPublisher` on it with `<odom_publish_frequency>1000</odom_publish_frequency>`. A message has to go out within the first 10 updates. With a lower rate and a 1 ms step, the rolling mean (10 samples) has dropped the first sample before the first message.
2. `gz topic -e -t /model/<name>/odometry`
3. Look at the `twist` of the first messages.

A fix and a test are in a pull request that follows.
